ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style, with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening and Q&A, contrasted with long, structured presentation turns. Participants frequently overlap lightly, especially during greetings, acknowledgments, and follow-up questions; interruptions are generally cooperative rather than competitive. Speech is informal and heavily disfluent, with repeated words, self-corrections, false starts, “um,” “yeah,” “okay,” “you know,” and unfinished phrasing, particularly from nonnative speakers and during technical explanations. Speakers hedge often with phrases like “I think,” “maybe,” “sort of,” “probably,” “I guess,” and “it could be,” framing claims as provisional. Questions tend to begin warmly—complimenting the talk or calling a question “naive”—then develop into multipart, exploratory prompts. Challenges are indirect and curiosity-driven: participants point out alternatives, limitations, or apparent tensions without adversarial language, and presenters respond expansively, acknowledge uncertainty, and connect the question to future work. Formal presentation segments use clear signposting and recap language, while transitions and social chat remain relaxed, friendly, and lightly humorous.

Meeting style for this meeting (running_out_of_time): The meeting starts late or the agenda is too long. People keep an eye on the clock, cut themselves off, skip items, and the meeting ends with things unfinished. No final recap.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - We've got maybe fifteen minutes, so- can we skip the intro stuff?
  - Yeah, sure. Let's just start with what's blocking.
  - I really have to jump in about five, sorry.
Opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Assessing whether forest carbon credits actually protect forest and who gets to decide how that is measured. Ecology contributes baselines, leakage, forest inventory and remote sensing, and permanence; political science contributes governance and enforcement, land tenure, and state versus local authority; science and technology studies contributes analysis of how a number becomes a credit, the role of auditors and certifiers, and whose knowledge counts.

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Rivera
speakers.background: A fourth-year ecology PhD candidate with seven years of combined field and geospatial research experience in tropical and subtropical forests. Her work combines permanent-plot inventory data, Landsat and Sentinel canopy-loss products, biomass models, and spatial matching to evaluate avoided-deforestation claims. She has contributed to wildfire-risk and carbon-reversal assessments for restoration and conservation projects, but has not led large multi-site field campaigns.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Rivera treats a credit’s environmental validity as a counterfactual and time-dependent inference problem: observed forest cover is not equivalent to avoided loss. She will distinguish canopy change from carbon stock change, press for plausible baseline construction, and ask whether displacement of clearing, fire exposure, and other reversal risks have been accounted for. She is cautious about claims derived solely from governance narratives or project paperwork when ecological measurements and uncertainty bounds are weak.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Dr. Samuel Okafor
speakers.background: A fifth-year political science PhD candidate studying environmental governance and land politics in forested regions. He has conducted document analysis, comparative case research, and semi-structured interviews with subnational officials, customary authorities, civil-society organizations, and conservation implementers. His dissertation examines how formal tenure rules, de facto access arrangements, enforcement capacity, and benefit-sharing institutions shape the implementation of land-use policy.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Okafor frames carbon projects as institutions embedded in overlapping jurisdictions rather than as technical interventions operating on a neutral landscape. He will ask who holds enforceable rights to exclude, use, monitor, or contest land-use decisions; how state and local authority are divided; and whether benefits and enforcement obligations are allocated in ways that affect implementation. He will resist treating any governance feature as causally decisive without a credible comparative strategy and evidence about how authority operates in practice.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Mei Chen
speakers.background: A third-year STS PhD candidate with prior experience as a research assistant on studies of environmental standards, audit trails, and public accountability. She uses close reading of protocols and project documents, process tracing, and interviews to examine how technical classifications are assembled and defended. Her current work follows how carbon-accounting rules move among project developers, validation bodies, certifiers, registries, and public reporting systems.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen examines credits as the outcome of a chain of translations: forest observations, maps, assumptions, and local accounts are made into standardized evidence, then into a number that can be issued and traded. She will ask which protocols define what counts as sufficient proof, what auditors and certifiers can challenge, what remains hidden in documentation, and whose knowledge is accepted or excluded when project boundaries and baselines are validated. She is still working out how best to connect this institutional analysis to ecological assessment without reducing either to the other.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run an initial project-scoping meeting. The participants should agree on the main research question: "Under what ecological, governance, and accounting conditions do forest carbon credits correspond to durable, additional forest protection, and who has authority to define and verify those conditions?" Rivera should explain that remote sensing can detect observed canopy change but cannot by itself establish the counterfactual baseline, leakage, or permanence. Okafor should identify land tenure, enforcement authority, and the division of state and local decision-making as potentially consequential, without claiming a known causal result. Chen should emphasize that protocols, auditors, certifiers, and documentation translate forest observations into credits and may privilege some forms of evidence over others. The group should discuss realistic sources and constraints: project documents and issuance records are public; field access, local interviews, and some audit materials require permission; an 18-month study cannot conduct intensive field inventories at many sites. They should not settle on a full design, site selection, causal conclusion, or community-engagement protocol. The meeting should leave room for the evaluated AI to generate interdisciplinary follow-up research questions about mechanisms, comparisons, evidence, affected decision-makers, and feasible study design.

required_follow_up_question_themes.integration: Ask how baseline or counterfactual deforestation assumptions are selected, validated, and contested; connect ecological model assumptions and remote-sensing evidence with standard-setter, auditor, government, and local/community authority.

required_follow_up_question_themes.theme: Leakage across jurisdictions and tenure regimes
required_follow_up_question_themes.integration: Ask whether displaced deforestation or extraction is detectable beyond project boundaries and how tenure, enforcement capacity, and state-local jurisdictional arrangements shape both leakage and responsibility for it.

Ask how fire, drought, harvesting, and future land-use risks are measured over time; connect ecological permanence indicators with contractual liability, buffer-pool rules, enforcement, and decision authority when reversals occur.

Ask what local observations or land-use knowledge could reveal that inventories, satellite products, or project records miss, and how protocols, auditors, and consent/governance arrangements determine whether such evidence counts.

Ask how a project moves from forest observations through baseline calculations, validation, verification, and issuance, and at which stages methodological choices could change credit quantities or claims of additional protection.

Ask which small number of contrasting projects or jurisdictions can be studied within 18 months, using public project and issuance records plus targeted permissions for field checks and interviews; identify what inference remains limited without access to audit materials or field sites.

Remote sensing alone cannot establish additionality, baseline validity, leakage, or permanence.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: Before we start—did the folder with the latest project design documents ever come through after last week? I may have missed it. Given the time, I was hoping today we could just establish what the public record can tell us, and where permissions, especially for local and state interviews, will become the binding constraint, rather than choosing sites already.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: I did get the folder, yes, though I haven't gone through every annex yet. On my first pass, the public files tell us the issued numbers and the stated baseline logic, but not always the evidence reviewers saw or why local land-use accounts were treated as adequate. So I’d want to separate- I’d want to distinguish missing public documentation from genuinely missing scrutiny.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: Mei, when an auditor or certifier accepts a map or a land-use claim, what can a state agency or residents actually do to challenge the evidence that went into that record? I ask because I'm already seeing the same area described as state-managed forest in one document and, sorry, I lost my point for a second. In another it's described as customary-use land, and there's no account of how that conflict was adjudicated.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: Mm, that’s worrying.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: Procedurally, it depends on the standard and the project stage. Often residents or an agency can submit comments or a grievance, but that isn't the same as having standing to get the map redone. I'd want to trace the exact path in a couple of cases, who receives an objection, what evidence they have to consider, and whether the response is public, because the documents can make a dispute disappear into a line saying "stakeholders consulted."

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: That distinction matters a great deal. A grievance channel without any obligation to reopen the evidentiary record isn't really a way to contest the allocation of authority. It's, um, closer to notification. Could we see in the public files whether objections trigger any response at all, and whether state agencies have a different procedural position from residents or customary authorities?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: I think we can see part of that, yes, but we should be careful about treating silence as no objection. The public record may show a consultation log, a formal comment period, maybe a grievance outcome. It may not show informal challenges or material sent directly to the validator. Could we make a small matrix for the candidate cases? I'm losing the thread a little, but who could object, through which channel, whether a reasoned response is required, and what actually appears publicly?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, I think that's useful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: Could that matrix also include the ecological record, like what baseline evidence is public, what monitoring imagery or plot data gets cited, and whether the claimed leakage or reversal risk is actually quantified? I’m asking because a project can have a very tidy consultation trail but still have a baseline that makes stable canopy look like additional protection.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: I think that's the right way to use it, not as two parallel checklists. For each case, we could ask where the ecological inputs enter the accounting record, which imagery, plots, and assumptions are cited, who reviewed them, and whether a challenge to the map could also challenge the baseline or the leakage claim. Otherwise we may- we could miss that the same boundary is doing several jobs at once.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: And because we only have 18 months, I'd keep the matrix to maybe two or three deliberately contrasting cases. Rather than trying to code every project. I also need to check whether the public imagery has enough cloud-free observations at the boundaries. Otherwise, a reported leakage pattern, or stable canopy, could just be a product-resolution problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: That sounds sensible. Before we settle the cases, though, I need to check a fairly basic thing. Whether the validation and verification reports actually include the underlying reviewer comments or just a final finding. If those aren't public, then our matrix should- it should mark that as an access condition, rather than implying the review was absent.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: Hm, that’s an important distinction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: And that access condition isn't just technical. If we can't see the underlying comments, we may not be able to tell whether a tenure conflict or a local challenge was considered and rejected, or whether it never reached the reviewer at all. I'd want the matrix to distinguish those two possibilities, rather than coding both as no evidence of contestation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: Exactly. We could use separate labels. No public trace of a challenge, a challenge documented but the evidence unavailable, and a documented review with reasons given. And I wouldn't assume the validator is the only doorway. Some standards route complaints through the registry or developer, and I'd need to check that case by case, but...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: And on the ecological side, I think we need that same distinction. No public trace that leakage or reversal was assessed isn't evidence it was ignored. But if the underlying analysis is inaccessible, we shouldn't let the final verification statement stand in as evidence that the baseline— or, say, edge displacement— that it was actually robust.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: And perhaps the governance column should not just record tenure as a legal category, but whether anyone has an enforceable capacity to contest a boundary or prevent clearing in practice. A state designation and customary use can coexist on paper, but the question is whose, whose claim becomes operative when the project's monitoring or benefit obligations are disputed.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: Yes, and that practical enforceability may be part of the ecological counterfactual, not just context. If restrictions can't actually be applied at a contested edge, then projecting the project's historical clearing rate forward as its baseline is pretty hard to defend. Though I'd want to see how those disputes map onto observed small clearings before making that, uh, claim.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: Exactly. I’d be cautious, though, about treating observed small clearings as a straightforward proxy for contestation or weak enforcement. They may reflect livelihood use that was never within the project’s enforceable authority in the first place. Could we at least, in the public-record pass, note what each document says about who’s authorized to enforce at those edges, and where that’s simply unresolved?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: I'd put that in, and keep the observation separate from the inference. Documented enforcement authority, reported use rights, and then what the canopy and disturbance data actually show near the edge. I'm especially wary of coding an edge as "leakage" before we know whether the activity was ever plausibly inside the project's counterfactual, or whether our imagery can even resolve those small clearings.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: And from the documents side, I’d resist calling those activities leakage until we can see how the project itself classified seasonal use and small-scale clearing when it drew the boundary. If a map turns customary-use space into an external “risk area,” that’s already an accounting, uh, decision, not just something the satellite later observes. I’m not sure the public files will let us reconstruct that, but it’s useful to flag.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: It may be worth treating that classification itself as a variable in the comparison. What the documents designate as project forest, leakage belt, or outside pressure, versus where we see disturbance accumulating. I don't think we can infer motive from that pattern, but it would tell us where the accounting boundary is doing ecological work and where we'd need field or local accounts before interpreting it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: And that comparison may expose a governance question before we infer anything from the disturbance pattern. Who had the authority to classify a customary-use area as external pressure rather than part of the project landscape? I'd add a field for the decision-maker and any stated basis for that classification. If we can't recover it publicly, that's precisely an interview-access dependency, not an- not an absence of authority.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: Mm, yes, that’s key.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: I think the public-record pass can make that visible without pretending it answers the question. For each classification, we note who is named as deciding, what evidence or consultation is cited, and whether there is any route to contest it. Then the blank spaces become pretty concrete questions for any later permission request, instead of us filling them in from the maps.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: Yeah—otherwise we risk treating the accounting categories as ecological facts.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Okafor
transcript.text: I think that’s enough for today, and we’re at time. Thank you both. Let’s, let’s pick this up once we’ve had a chance to look more closely at what the public record actually contains.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: Thanks, both. Bye for now.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rivera
transcript.text: All right, speak soon.
